claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is governed by the interplay between severe lattice distortion and interface-localized chemical short-range order.
Severe lattice distortion promotes dislocation nucleation.
Severe lattice distortion impedes long-range dislocation glide.
Enhanced CSRO at layer interfaces acts as a barrier to dislocation motion.
Dislocations nucleate preferentially in layers with relatively low local chemical ordering.
The mismatch between easier intralayer nucleation and impeded interface crossing causes strain to accumulate at the interfaces.
Increasing duration of sustained loading causes a gradual transition from extended dislocation glide to localized shear banding and possible interface amorphization.
The starting coating consists of alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers.
Early deformation is dislocation-mediated and largely confined within individual layers.
At longer creep times, localized shear bands and incipient amorphous zones develop at the interfaces.
The proposed transition enables progressive deformation while retaining a balance between strength and deformation tolerance.
Interface shear bands and amorphous zones produce a smoother strain distribution and lower stress concentration than in conventional metallic multilayers.
The proposed deformation response permits sustained deformation without catastrophic failure.
Conventional metallic multilayers typically exhibit abrupt planar dislocation glide and localized strain concentration leading to premature failure.
High-entropy multilayers have a more distributed plastic response than conventional metallic multilayers because of chemical complexity and lattice distortion.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the nanoscale multilayer architecture and interface chemical heterogeneity are retained.
Bulk diffusion or phase mixing that homogenizes the interfaces will suppress the proposed mechanism.
Samples with enhanced interface CSRO should exhibit different creep behavior and interface-localized deformation from samples with minimized CSRO under otherwise identical conditions.
The proposed behavior is expected under constant stress at room-to-moderately elevated temperatures, provided substantial intermixing is avoided.
